m4-rc1.title: Passage: The value of boredom
m4-rc1.html:
Passage: The value of boredom

Boredom has a poor reputation. It is treated as a problem to be solved, by entertainment for the young and by productivity tools for adults, and the devices most of us carry are designed to ensure that we need never experience it. Yet psychologists who study boredom increasingly describe it not as an absence of feeling but as a signal, comparable to hunger or pain, that tells us something about our situation.

What boredom signals, on this account, is a mismatch between the attention we have available and the demands our circumstances make on it. When a task is too easy, too repetitive or too disconnected from anything we value, attention has nowhere useful to go, and the resulting discomfort pushes us to look for something else. Like hunger, the signal is unpleasant precisely so that it will be acted upon. A person who never felt bored would have no reason to leave an unrewarding activity.

If this is right, the habit of silencing boredom the moment it appears has a hidden cost. The signal is answered, but by the nearest available stimulus rather than by a change in what one is doing. A worker who checks her phone whenever a meeting drags has relieved the discomfort without asking whether the meeting, or her role in it, should change. Repeated often enough, such relief may weaken the link between the signal and the reflection it is supposed to prompt.

Psychologists who study boredom have found that people do not experience it uniformly. Some report it rarely even in dull circumstances, while others find it oppressive in situations that their companions consider pleasant enough. The difference does not seem to lie in how much stimulation each person requires so much as in how well each can direct attention: those who struggle to concentrate find it harder to engage with a task that offers little, and so experience its emptiness more acutely. On this view boredom is less a property of situations than a relation between a situation and a mind's capacity to take hold of it.

This helps explain why boredom is unpleasant rather than merely neutral. An empty hour is not in itself painful; what hurts is the sense that one's attention is idling while something else ought to be happening. Boredom thus contains a kind of judgement, however vague, that the present activity is not worth the attention it demands, and its discomfort is the pressure of that judgement towards a change.

Some writers go further and claim that boredom is the mother of creativity: that the mind, left without stimulation, turns inward and produces new ideas. The evidence for this stronger claim is thinner than its popularity suggests. Studies that induce boredom before a creative task have found modest effects at best, and it is unclear whether they reflect boredom itself or merely the relief of being given something to do. The more defensible position is that boredom is useful as information, not as a source of inspiration — and information is valuable only to those who pause long enough to read it.

m4-rc2.title: Passage: Who owns a recipe
m4-rc2.html:
Passage: Who owns a recipe

Recipes occupy an odd place in the law of creative work. A novel, a song or a photograph is protected from copying as soon as it is made, but in most legal systems a list of ingredients and a set of cooking steps are treated as functional instructions, like the directions for assembling a bookcase, and may be copied freely. A chef who invents a celebrated dish can watch competitors reproduce it the following week without any legal remedy.

Economic theory suggests that this should discourage invention. If creators cannot exclude imitators, why would they invest in creating? Yet restaurant cuisine is notably inventive, and new dishes appear constantly. Researchers who have studied professional kitchens find that chefs rely on informal norms in place of law. Copying a dish exactly without acknowledgement is widely regarded as disreputable, and chefs who do it may find that suppliers, critics and colleagues treat them coolly. Sharing techniques with trusted peers is expected, but passing them on to outsiders without permission is frowned upon.

These norms are effective in a small, interconnected community where reputation travels quickly. They work less well across distances, in large chains, or where the copier has no wish to belong to the community whose disapproval would otherwise restrain him. A chain that reproduces a famous chef's dish across hundreds of outlets may never meet the chef's peers and has little to fear from their opinion.

The fashion industry offers an instructive comparison. Clothing designs, like recipes, receive limited protection in many legal systems, and copying is rapid and widespread. Here too the field is inventive, and some scholars have argued that copying actually accelerates the cycle of fashion: once a style is widely imitated it loses its distinction, and those who wish to stand out must move on to something new. Whether the same mechanism operates in cooking is unclear. A dish does not lose its pleasure merely because others serve it, and diners who return to a favourite restaurant often want the same meal rather than a novelty. The analogy shows that the absence of protection need not stifle creation, but it does not show that the reasons are the same in every field.

Chefs themselves are divided. Some regard imitation as a tribute and a sign that their influence is spreading; others, particularly those whose reputation rests on a small number of signature dishes, see it as a threat to their livelihood. The division often tracks the chef's position in the profession: established figures can afford generosity, while newcomers who have staked everything on one idea have the most to lose from its free circulation.

Some observers conclude that the law should be extended to cover recipes. Others argue that the absence of protection is itself a cause of the field's inventiveness: chefs who cannot rest on a single creation must keep producing new ones, and the free circulation of ideas allows each innovation to be built upon quickly. The evidence does not settle the question, but it does show that the relationship between legal protection and creativity is less direct than the simple economic model assumes.

m4-rc3.title: Passage: Counting the uncounted species
m4-rc3.html:
Passage: Counting the uncounted species

Estimates of the number of species on Earth range from a few million to more than a trillion, a spread that would be embarrassing in almost any other science. The disagreement does not arise because biologists are careless. It arises because the great majority of species have never been described, and the methods for estimating what has not been seen depend heavily on assumptions about it.

One method extrapolates from well-studied groups. If, in a thoroughly surveyed region, there are a certain number of insect species for every species of plant, and if this ratio holds elsewhere, the global count of plants can be multiplied to give a global count of insects. The approach is transparent, but its results are only as good as the ratio, and ratios measured in temperate forests may not hold in tropical canopies or deep-sea sediments. Another method looks at the rate at which new species are described over time and projects when the curve will level off. This method assumes that taxonomists' efforts have been spread evenly, when in practice they have concentrated on large, attractive or economically important organisms.

The arrival of genetic sequencing has changed the problem rather than solved it. Sampling soil or seawater for DNA reveals vast numbers of distinct genetic sequences, many belonging to microbes that have never been grown in a laboratory. But deciding how different two sequences must be to count as separate species is partly a matter of convention, and different thresholds can change totals by orders of magnitude. The trillion-species estimates depend largely on such counts of microbial diversity.

The difficulty is not only practical. Even among well-studied animals, biologists disagree about what a species is. One definition counts as a species any group whose members can interbreed with one another but not with outsiders; another counts any population with a distinct evolutionary history, which can be detected in its genes even when it looks identical to its neighbours. The second definition typically yields more species than the first, and the choice between them is guided as much by the purposes of the classifier as by anything in the organisms. Conservation agencies, for instance, have an interest in recognising distinct populations that would otherwise be grouped with abundant relatives and so denied protection.

For organisms that reproduce without sex, as most microbes do, the interbreeding definition does not apply at all, and the genetic threshold is the only practical criterion. Changing that threshold by a small amount can merge thousands of supposed species into one or split one into thousands, which is why the largest estimates are so sensitive to choices that seem, at first sight, merely technical.

What these difficulties show is not that the question is meaningless but that "how many species are there?" is several questions at once. For animals and plants, estimates are converging on figures in the low millions. For microbes, the answer depends on definitions that have been designed for other purposes and may not suit the organisms in question. A single headline number conceals these differences more than it reveals them.

m4-rc4.title: Passage: The architecture of waiting rooms
m4-rc4.html:
Passage: The architecture of waiting rooms

Waiting rooms are among the most widely experienced and least considered spaces in modern life. Clinics, government offices and railway stations all require people to spend time in rooms whose design rarely receives the attention given to the spaces where the main business happens. The assumption seems to be that waiting is dead time, and that a room for dead time needs only seats and perhaps a clock.

Yet a waiting room shapes how people experience the service that follows. Studies in clinics have found that patients who wait in crowded, windowless rooms with no indication of how long they will wait rate their consultations less favourably, even when the consultation itself is identical. Uncertainty seems to matter more than duration: a predictable twenty-minute wait is often reported as less irritating than an unpredictable ten-minute one. Information about queue length, and a sense that the order of service is fair, can do more to improve satisfaction than shortening the wait itself.

Design also communicates status. Rows of fixed seating facing a counter suggest that those waiting are to be processed; movable chairs, natural light and somewhere to put one's belongings suggest that they are guests. People read these signals quickly and adjust their expectations and behaviour accordingly. Staff in offices with hostile waiting areas report more confrontations, though whether the design causes the hostility or merely reflects an institution that already treats visitors poorly is difficult to establish.

Many of the improvements that matter cost little. A screen that shows the number of people ahead in line, or an announcement that the clinic is running thirty minutes late, gives people the means to plan: to make a phone call, fetch a coffee or simply stop watching the door. Seating arranged in small clusters rather than long rows allows families to sit together and strangers to keep their distance. Even the placement of the reception desk matters; a counter behind glass, raised above the level of a seated visitor, tells people something different from a desk at which they can sit down and speak face to face.

Some institutions have gone further and abolished the waiting room altogether, sending visitors a message when their turn approaches so that they can wait wherever they please. Such systems are welcome where they work, but they assume that visitors have phones, can read the messages and have somewhere else to go. For many people who use public services, the waiting room remains the only place available, and its design continues to shape what the visit feels like.

Architects who have worked on such spaces note that the brief they receive rarely mentions waiting at all. Budgets and attention are allocated to the consulting room, the counter or the platform, and the waiting area is whatever space is left over once those have been placed.

Improving waiting rooms is cheap compared with improving the services they precede, which makes it tempting to dismiss such improvements as cosmetic. But a service is experienced as a whole, and an institution that respects people's time before they reach the counter has already begun to deliver part of what they came for.

m5-rc1.title: Passage: The persistence of the QWERTY argument
m5-rc1.html:
Passage: The persistence of the QWERTY argument

For several decades the arrangement of keys on the standard typewriter keyboard served economists as the leading example of a market locking in an inferior technology. The story ran as follows. The layout was designed for mechanical reasons that soon ceased to matter; a rival layout allowed faster typing; but because typists trained on the standard and employers bought machines for trained typists, no one could switch alone, and the worse design survived. The example was vivid and widely taught.

Later historians questioned almost every part of it. The evidence that the rival layout was faster turned out to rest on a few small studies, some conducted by its own inventor, and later comparisons found little difference. Typing speed depends much more on training than on the arrangement of keys. If the rival was not clearly better, then the market had not locked in an inferior product; it had simply kept a perfectly adequate one.

The interesting question is why the original story spread so far on so little evidence. Part of the answer is that it illustrated a theoretical possibility that economists wanted to discuss. Models showing that markets could become stuck with worse standards were elegant and plausible, and a concrete case made them easier to teach. Once the example was in textbooks, it was repeated rather than checked, each citation lending authority to the next.

The revision did not go unchallenged. Defenders of the original account replied that the absence of clear evidence for the rival layout's superiority did not prove that the two were equal; small studies are weak in both directions, and a layout that had never been widely adopted could not be tested on the large population of experienced typists who would reveal its advantages, if it had any. The point has some force, but it cuts against the original story as much as for it. An example offered as a demonstration of market failure needs evidence that the rejected alternative was better, and a demonstration that rests on the impossibility of testing its central claim is not much of a demonstration.

Other candidate examples of lock-in have fared similarly when examined closely. Rival formats in recording, competing gauges on early railways and alternative designs for nuclear reactors have each been offered as cases in which an inferior option prevailed through historical accident. In each, historians have found reasons, sometimes technical and sometimes commercial, why the winner was a reasonable choice at the time, and the evidence that the loser was clearly better has usually been thinner than the story required. None of these findings disproves the theory. They suggest only that clean real-world cases are rarer than the theory's popularity would lead one to expect.

None of this shows that lock-in never happens. Standards do become entrenched, and switching costs are real. What the episode shows is that a good illustration can outrun its evidence, and that the more neatly an example fits a theory, the less likely it is to be examined. The lesson applies well beyond economics. Disciplines tend to keep a small stock of famous cases, and the fame of a case is not a reliable guide to its accuracy.

m5-rc2.title: Passage: Learning from failure in aviation
m5-rc2.html:
Passage: Learning from failure in aviation

Commercial aviation is often held up as a model of learning from failure. Accidents are investigated by independent bodies whose findings are published, and pilots are encouraged to report their own errors and near misses without fear of punishment. The result, admirers say, is that every crash makes the next one less likely. Hospitals, courts and other institutions are urged to copy the approach.

The admiration is deserved, but the lessons are harder to transfer than they appear. Aviation enjoys several advantages that are rarely mentioned in the exhortations. Its failures are dramatic and public, so there is strong pressure to explain them. Its systems are highly standardised: aircraft of the same type are nearly identical, and procedures are written in detail, so a lesson drawn from one incident applies directly to thousands of flights. And the people whose errors are reported — pilots — are themselves at risk when things go wrong, which aligns their interests with safety.

Many other fields lack these features. A medical error may harm a single patient privately and be noticed, if at all, much later. Patients differ from one another far more than aircraft do, so a lesson from one case may not apply to the next. And the professional who errs is rarely the one who suffers the consequences. Under such conditions, a reporting system modelled on aviation may collect many reports without producing the cumulative improvement it promises.

The contrast is visible within medicine itself. Anaesthesia, which resembles aviation more than most specialties do, with standardised equipment, a sequence of well-defined steps and constant monitoring by instruments, adopted checklists and incident reporting early and saw marked improvements in safety. Areas of medicine where each case presents differently, and where judgement rather than procedure governs much of the work, have found the same tools harder to apply. The difference is not that one group of doctors cares more about safety than another. It is that the conditions under which reporting produces learning are present in one setting and largely absent in the other.

Reporting systems also depend on trust, and trust is easier to promise than to secure. A professional who reports an error must believe that the report will be used to improve the system rather than to assign blame, and that belief is fragile. A single case in which a report is used against the person who filed it can undo years of encouragement, and in fields where litigation is common, the fear of such use may never be overcome. Those who praise aviation's openness sometimes forget how much institutional work went into making it safe to be open.

This does not mean other fields should ignore aviation's example. It means that what they should borrow is less a procedure than a principle: that errors are signs of weaknesses in systems rather than simply failures of individuals. How to act on that principle will depend on features of each field — how visible its failures are, how standardised its work, how aligned the interests of those involved — that no imported procedure can supply.

m5-rc3.title: Passage: Urban noise and birdsong
m5-rc3.html:
Passage: Urban noise and birdsong

Birds that live in cities sing differently from their rural relatives. In several species, urban males sing at higher pitch, louder, or at different times of day, often starting before dawn traffic begins. The most widely accepted explanation is masking: the low-frequency rumble of traffic drowns out lower notes, so birds that shift upward are heard more easily by mates and rivals.

The explanation is plausible, and experiments support part of it. When researchers play recordings of traffic noise near singing birds, some individuals raise their pitch within minutes, which shows that the change can be a flexible response rather than an inherited trait. But other findings complicate the picture. Higher notes do not carry as far as lower ones, so a bird that escapes masking may still be heard over a smaller area. And in some species, females prefer lower songs, which are associated with larger, healthier males. A male that sings higher to be heard may become less attractive to those who hear him.

These trade-offs suggest that urban song is not simply an improvement forced by noise but a compromise, whose terms vary with the density of the population, the structure of the habitat and the preferences of the listeners. Where birds live close together, a short-range signal may be enough; where they are sparse, the loss of range may matter more than the gain in clarity.

Timing offers a different escape from noise. Some urban birds have shifted their singing earlier in the morning, before traffic builds, or later into the evening, and a few have been recorded singing at night near brightly lit roads. Here too the adjustment has costs. Singing in the dark exposes a bird to predators that hunt by sound and may cut into the time it needs to rest and feed, and it may not coincide with the hours when females are most attentive. A shift that solves the problem of masking can thus create problems of its own, just as a shift in pitch does.

There is also the question of whether urban populations are diverging from rural ones in ways that go beyond flexible adjustment. Young birds of many species learn their songs by listening to adults, so a population that sings higher may pass the higher song to the next generation through learning alone, without any change in its genes. Over many generations, a learned difference of this kind could make urban and rural birds less responsive to one another's songs, and some researchers have suggested that this may be a first step towards the separation of populations. The evidence for such divergence is still preliminary, and other researchers caution that birds moving between city and countryside would tend to blur any difference that began to form.

The study of urban song has broader interest because it shows how quickly behaviour can respond to environments transformed by people. It also shows how misleading a single explanation can be. A change that looks like a straightforward adaptation may involve costs that are hidden unless one asks who is listening, from how far away, and with what preferences.

m5-rc4.title: Passage: The meaning of a signature
m5-rc4.html:
Passage: The meaning of a signature

Signatures were once the chief way of binding a person to a document. A name written by hand was hard to forge convincingly, and its presence on a page signalled that the signer had seen and accepted what was written there. Today most agreements are made with a click, a typed name or a box ticked on a screen, and the handwritten signature survives mainly for occasions that people regard as solemn: marriages, property sales, wills.

It is tempting to see this survival as nostalgia, but it serves a purpose. The effort of signing, small as it is, marks a transition from considering to committing. People sign fewer things than they click, and the act draws attention to the fact that something consequential is happening. Legal scholars call this the cautionary function of formalities: requirements that slow people down so that they notice what they are doing.

Digital agreements have largely abandoned this function in pursuit of convenience. A user who accepts the terms of a service may do so dozens of times a week, and the click that binds her is identical to the click that dismisses an advertisement. The law generally treats such clicks as valid consent, but few people believe they represent the considered acceptance that the older form was meant to secure.

The history of formalities suggests that they have always been a compromise between caution and convenience. Wax seals, witnesses and notaries each slowed the making of agreements and each was relaxed when commerce demanded speed. Legal systems responded by distinguishing between transactions: ordinary sales could be made by word of mouth, while gifts of land or promises without payment required writing, witnesses or both. The distinction rested on the observation that people are most likely to act rashly when they give something away or bind their future selves, and that these were the cases in which a moment of ceremony was most valuable.

Digital systems have largely collapsed this distinction. The same interface is used to accept a trivial licence and to consent to the sharing of medical records, and the user is given no signal that one matters more than the other. Some of the difficulty is commercial: firms that profit from frictionless consent have little reason to introduce ceremony. But some of it reflects a genuine uncertainty about which online agreements deserve a pause, since their consequences are often hidden in terms that few users read and fewer understand.

Some designers propose restoring friction to important digital agreements: requiring users to type a phrase, wait a few seconds or confirm twice. Critics reply that friction will soon become habitual and that people will learn to perform it as absent-mindedly as they now click. The disagreement turns on whether the cautionary effect of formalities comes from the effort itself or from its rarity. If rarity is what matters, adding friction to every agreement would defeat the purpose; it would work only if reserved for the agreements that genuinely deserve it.

b12-rows.title: Two facing rows (Easy)
b12-rows.html:
Two facing rows

Six friends — Amit, Bhavna, Charu, Deepak, Ela and Firoz — sit in two rows of three seats. The north row faces south and the south row faces north, so each person directly faces one person in the other row.

b16-rc1.title: Telling more than we can know
b16-rc1.html:
Telling more than we can know

Ask people why they chose one of several identical pairs of stockings laid out on a table, and they will give reasons readily: this pair felt softer, that one had a better sheen. In a well-known set of experiments, the pairs really were identical, and the choice was driven mostly by position: people tended to prefer whichever item lay furthest to the right. Yet almost nobody mentioned position, and when it was suggested to them, most denied it firmly. They were not lying. They sincerely believed the reasons they gave.

Findings of this kind have led some psychologists to a startling conclusion: that we have far less direct access to the causes of our own behaviour than we suppose. On this view, when we explain our choices we are not reading off a report from some inner observatory. We are doing what an outsider would do: drawing on a stock of plausible theories about why people act as they do, and applying the one that seems to fit. The tell-tale sign is that our explanations of our own behaviour are often no more accurate than the explanations a stranger would offer for us, and are wrong in the same ways.

It would be easy to overstate the point. The experiments show that people can be mistaken about causes they have no reason to notice, such as the position of an item on a table. They do not show that we are wrong about everything inside us. A person in pain generally knows that she is in pain, and someone working through a sum in her head can usually say which step she is on. What the research undermines is not self-knowledge in general but a particular confidence: the belief that when we can produce a reason for an action, the reason we produce is the one that moved us.

That confidence matters, because so much of social life depends on the reasons people give. We ask job candidates why they want the post, witnesses why they noticed what they did, and voters why they prefer one candidate. If the answers are partly constructions, assembled after the fact from the stock of available theories, then they tell us less about the person than we assume, and more about what that person, and the culture around her, regards as a respectable reason.

There is a further and less comfortable implication. If our explanations are theories, they can be improved, as theories can, but only by evidence that comes from outside. The person who wishes to know why she really avoids certain colleagues may learn more from a careful record of when she does so than from any amount of reflection. Introspection, on this account, is not useless, but it is a source of hypotheses rather than of verdicts, and it deserves the same scepticism we bring to any hypothesis that flatters the person who holds it.

b16-rc2.title: The second life of clothes
b16-rc2.html:
The second life of clothes

Every year, bales of used clothing donated in wealthy countries are sorted, compressed and shipped to markets in East and West Africa, where traders buy them unseen and resell the contents piece by piece. For the donor the transaction ends at the collection bin and feels like charity. For the economies at the other end it is something more complicated: a large, unregulated trade that has been blamed for destroying local textile industries and praised for clothing millions of people cheaply.

The case against the trade is usually made through history. In the decades after independence, several countries built clothing and textile factories that employed tens of thousands of workers. Many of those factories have since closed, and their decline coincided with a flood of imported second-hand clothing. Critics draw the obvious conclusion and some governments have acted on it, proposing high tariffs or outright bans on used garments in the hope of reviving domestic production.

The conclusion is less obvious than it looks. The same decades saw other changes that hurt local factories at least as much: the removal of protective tariffs under structural adjustment programmes, unreliable electricity, and above all the arrival of very cheap new clothing from Asia. Studies that try to separate these causes generally find that second-hand imports played a real but partial role. A ban on used clothing, on this evidence, would be more likely to open the market to cheap new imports than to bring back the old factories.

Meanwhile the trade itself supports a dense web of livelihoods. Importers sell bales to wholesalers, who sell them to market traders, who employ tailors to alter, mend and restyle what they buy. Because no trader knows what a bale contains until it is opened, the business resembles a lottery in which skill lies in judging suppliers, spotting quality and repairing what others would discard. Those who make a living this way are not victims of the trade but its practitioners, and their interests are seldom heard in debates conducted on their behalf.

None of this makes the trade benign. The quality of bales has declined as fast fashion has spread in the donor countries, so that a growing share of what arrives is too worn or too flimsy to sell. That share ends up in landfills and on riverbanks in the importing countries, which bear the cost of disposing of clothes that the donors have, in effect, exported rather than thrown away. The problem here is not that Africans buy used clothes but that rich countries consume clothing at a rate their own waste systems would struggle to absorb.

A useful debate would separate these questions. Whether used clothing harms local industry is an empirical matter, and the answer appears to be: somewhat, but less than other forces. Whether the trade's waste is fair is a question about responsibility, and the answer points back towards the donors' wardrobes rather than towards the markets that receive their castoffs.

b16-rc3.title: The invention of wilderness
b16-rc3.html:
The invention of wilderness

The great national parks of the nineteenth and twentieth centuries were founded on a picture of nature as a place without people. Their creators spoke of untouched landscapes, of country as it had been before human history began, and they drew boundaries to keep it that way. What they seldom acknowledged was that many of these landscapes had been inhabited, hunted, burned and managed for thousands of years, and that making them empty required removing the people who lived there.

Historians have since shown how much of the 'wilderness' that visitors admire is the product of that management. Open grasslands that early travellers took for natural features were often maintained by regular, deliberate burning; when the burning stopped after the inhabitants were expelled, forests crept in and the very scenery the parks had been created to protect began to change. In some places, the removal of grazing or of small-scale cultivation reduced rather than increased the variety of plants and animals.

None of this means that the founders were simply wrong to want to protect these places. The threats they saw, from logging, mining and settlement on an industrial scale, were real, and the parks did save landscapes that would otherwise have been destroyed. The error lay in the idea that protection meant the absence of people, and in the assumption that the people who were there did not count as part of what was being protected.

The idea persists in subtler forms. Conservation funding often flows more readily to projects that promise to keep areas 'intact', a word that quietly implies that human presence is a form of damage. Communities living inside or beside protected areas may be allowed to stay only on condition that they give up practices, such as seasonal burning or the collection of forest produce, that may have helped to shape the habitat in the first place. In such cases, conservation can end up undermining the very ecological conditions it aims to preserve.

The alternative is not to abolish protected areas but to rethink what they are for. If many valued landscapes are joint products of natural processes and long human use, then protecting them may require keeping some of that use going, and the people who know how to do it may be the most useful allies a park can have. Some parks have begun to work in this way, restoring traditional burning under the guidance of the communities that once practised it.

The lesson reaches beyond particular parks. The word 'wilderness' carries a story about human beings as outsiders to nature, visitors who can only spoil what they touch. That story has inspired admirable acts of protection. But a story in which people are always the problem makes it hard to imagine them as part of any solution, and it has fallen hardest on those whose presence in the landscape was longest.

b16-rc4.title: What a tip pays for
b16-rc4.html:
What a tip pays for

Tipping is one of the few economic customs that most of its participants claim to dislike and nearly all continue to practise. In countries where it is expected, diners complain about calculating percentages, workers complain about unpredictable earnings, and economists complain that the custom serves none of the purposes usually claimed for it. Yet attempts by restaurants to abolish tips and raise prices instead have often been abandoned within a year or two.

The standard defence of tipping is that it rewards good service. A waiter who knows that his income depends on the customer's satisfaction will, the argument goes, work harder to provide it. The evidence for this is surprisingly weak. Studies that compare the size of tips with diners' own ratings of the service usually find only a small connection between the two. Tips depend more on the size of the bill, the weather, whether the server introduced herself by name, and the diner's mood than on anything the server did with the food.

If tipping does little to discipline service, why does it survive? One answer is that it disguises prices. A menu without tips must show prices about a fifth higher, and customers comparing menus tend to choose the restaurant that looks cheaper, even when the final bill would be the same. A restaurant that abolishes tipping on its own therefore appears more expensive than its rivals, which is why such experiments have so often failed.

A second answer concerns the relationship between diner and server. Tipping lets the customer feel generous, and turns a commercial payment into something closer to a gift. Many people value that feeling, and some are willing to pay for it. The difficulty is that a gift, unlike a wage, can be withheld, and those who depend on it are exposed to the prejudices as well as the generosity of strangers. Research has repeatedly found that tips vary with servers' appearance, age and ethnicity in ways that have nothing to do with the quality of their work.

These two explanations suggest different remedies. If tipping survives mainly because it hides prices, then the solution lies in rules that require all-inclusive pricing for every restaurant at once, so that no single business is punished for honesty. If it survives because customers value the gesture of giving, then abolition may be neither achievable nor entirely desirable, and the task becomes to limit the damage, for instance by guaranteeing a base wage that does not depend on the gift.

In practice both forces are at work, which may explain why the custom has proved so durable. A practice that conceals prices from customers and offers them a pleasant feeling of generosity at the same time is unlikely to disappear through market pressure alone.

b16-rc5.title: Beauty as evidence
b16-rc5.html:
Beauty as evidence

Physicists often describe the theories they most admire as beautiful, and some have gone further, claiming that beauty is a reliable guide to truth. A theory that explains a wide range of phenomena from a few simple principles, with no arbitrary adjustments, is said to carry a mark of correctness, and history seems to offer support: several equations chosen for their elegance were later confirmed by experiment in ways their authors could not have foreseen.

Sceptics reply that this history is selective. For every elegant theory that was confirmed, there were others, equally admired in their day, that turned out to be false. Nobody remembers them because textbooks record the winners. Moreover, what counts as beautiful has changed. The circular orbits of early astronomy were admired for their perfection, and the ellipses that replaced them were at first thought ugly. If the standard of beauty shifts to accommodate whatever theories succeed, then beauty cannot be an independent test of success.

Defenders of the aesthetic criterion need not claim that beauty guarantees truth. A more modest version holds that, in the absence of decisive evidence, simplicity and economy are reasonable grounds for preferring one theory over another, because a theory with fewer adjustable parts makes sharper predictions and is easier to refute. On this view, elegance is valuable not as a sign that nature itself is beautiful but as a practical virtue: it keeps theories honest by limiting their ability to fit any result.

The difficulty arises when the modest version slides into the ambitious one. In some areas of modern physics, experiments that could decide between rival theories lie far beyond present technology, and may remain so for generations. In that situation it is tempting to let aesthetic judgement do the work of evidence, and to treat a theory's elegance as grounds for believing it rather than merely as grounds for investigating it further. Critics argue that whole research programmes have been sustained for decades in this way, absorbing talent and funding while producing no testable predictions.

The disagreement is not, at bottom, about whether beauty matters. Almost everyone agrees that it guides the choice of which ideas to pursue. It is about what happens when guidance hardens into conviction. A scientist who prefers a simple theory because it is easier to test is using elegance as a tool. A scientist who believes a theory because it is too beautiful to be wrong has made elegance a substitute for the test, and has, in a sense, left science for something closer to taste.

Whether that matters depends on whether the tests eventually arrive. If they do, the beautiful theory will be confirmed or refuted like any other, and the confidence placed in it will be judged by the result. If they never do, the field risks becoming a contest of aesthetic preferences in which the deciding votes belong to whoever holds the most influential positions.

b16-rc6.title: Minds in the sea
b16-rc6.html:
Minds in the sea

The octopus is an awkward animal for anyone who believes that intelligence is a mark of our own lineage. Its last common ancestor with humans was a small, probably worm-like creature that lived more than five hundred million years ago, long before either line had anything resembling a brain. Yet octopuses solve puzzles, use objects as tools, recognise individual people, and appear to play. Whatever intelligence they have, it evolved on its own, by a different route, in a body that could hardly be less like ours.

That body shapes the mind it carries. Most of an octopus's neurons are not in its central brain but in its arms, each of which can taste, touch and respond to what it encounters with a degree of independence. An arm severed from the body will still reach for food and attempt to pass it to a mouth that is no longer there. It is unclear what, if anything, it is like to be such an animal, but it is unlikely to resemble the single, centred point of view that we take for granted in ourselves.

These facts have become practical as well as philosophical. Proposals to farm octopuses on an industrial scale have prompted scientists and ethicists to ask whether the animals can suffer, and if so, what farming would mean for them. A government review in one country concluded that there was strong evidence of sentience in octopuses and their relatives, enough to bring them within animal-welfare law. The evidence included signs that injured octopuses tend their wounds, avoid places where they were hurt, and will accept a painkiller when one is offered.

Critics of the review pointed out that none of these behaviours proves that the animal feels anything. A sufficiently complicated machine might avoid damage and tend its injuries without any experience at all. This is true, but it proves less than the critics hope. The same could be said of any animal other than oneself; we infer that other mammals feel pain from just such behaviour, together with similarities of anatomy. In the octopus the anatomical similarity is missing, which makes the inference weaker, but the behavioural evidence is no less striking.

What, then, should follow from uncertainty? One view holds that we should extend protection only when sentience is established. The opposite view, increasingly influential, holds that when there is a realistic possibility that a creature can suffer, the burden of proof should fall on those who would subject it to conditions likely to cause suffering. The second view does not claim to know what the octopus feels. It claims that ignorance, in a matter where the possible harm is grave and the cost of caution modest, is a reason for restraint rather than a licence.

The octopus thus poses a test less of our science than of our habits of reasoning. We are used to extending moral concern along lines of resemblance. An animal whose mind may be rich but is certainly strange invites us to ask whether resemblance was ever the right guide.

b2-rc1.title: What de-extinction would restore
b2-rc1.html:
What de-extinction would restore

Each time a team of geneticists announces progress towards reviving an extinct animal, the headlines tend to promise a homecoming: the woolly mammoth back on the tundra, the passenger pigeon darkening American skies again. What is actually on offer is more modest and, in some ways, more interesting. No laboratory can recover a complete genome from remains that have lain in permafrost or museum drawers for centuries; DNA breaks into fragments, and the gaps must be filled from living relatives. The likely product is therefore not a mammoth but an elephant edited to carry a few dozen mammoth traits, such as dense hair and a thick layer of fat.

Supporters argue that this distinction matters less than it seems. What an ecosystem notices, they say, is not an animal's pedigree but what it does. If cold-adapted elephants trampled snow and toppled shrubs as mammoths once did, they might help restore the grassland that once covered much of the far north, which, some ecologists argue, keeps the ground beneath it colder than forest does. On this view, de-extinction is a tool for reviving lost ecological functions, and the name is merely a piece of marketing.

Critics accept the functional framing but draw the opposite conclusion from it. If the aim is to restore what an animal did, they ask, why begin with the most expensive and uncertain route? Many lost functions can be partly supplied by species that still exist: horses and bison have been released onto Siberian grassland for exactly this purpose. More pointedly, the money and attention that flow to spectacular revival projects may come at the expense of species that are declining now and could be saved by ordinary means, such as protecting habitat. There is also a worry about moral hazard. If extinction comes to seem reversible, the urgency of preventing it may fade.

Neither side, it should be said, has much evidence to offer yet. No edited animal has yet been set loose in the ecosystem it is meant to restore, so claims about ecological benefit remain projections, and the fear that revival will drain funds from conservation assumes that the money would otherwise have gone there, which is far from certain; much of it comes from private investors drawn by the novelty of the technology itself.

What the debate does reveal is how unclear the goal of conservation has become. For most of its history the field could define success as keeping species from disappearing. Once a species can, in some sense, be rebuilt, that definition no longer settles very much. We are pushed to say what we were trying to preserve all along: particular lineages of living things, the work they did in the world, or our own sense of what a complete landscape looks like.

b2-rc2.title: Why proverbs disagree
b2-rc2.html:
Why proverbs disagree

Collections of proverbs are full of contradictions. 'Look before you leap' sits uneasily beside 'he who hesitates is lost'; 'many hands make light work' is flatly denied by 'too many cooks spoil the broth'. To the systematic mind this looks like an embarrassment. A body of advice that recommends both caution and boldness, both cooperation and its avoidance, seems to recommend nothing at all.

The embarrassment fades once we ask what proverbs are for. They are not premises from which conclusions can be deduced, still less laws that hold in all cases. They are closer to tools, each suited to a recurring kind of situation. A carpenter is not inconsistent for owning both a saw and a glue pot; the question is never which tool is correct in general, but which one this job needs. A proverb is summoned when a speaker has already sized up a situation and wants to name it compactly, and the name carries a recommendation with it. The recommendation is only as good as the sizing-up that came before it: describe a hasty plan as bold and the proverb about hesitation blesses it; describe it as reckless and the proverb about looking first condemns it.

This means that the real knowledge lies not in the proverbs but in the judgement that selects among them, and that judgement is precisely what proverbs cannot supply. No proverb tells you whether the moment calls for looking or for leaping. Seen in this light, the oddity is not that proverbs contradict each other but that anyone expected them not to. A culture that offered only one of each pair would be giving worse advice, not better, because it would be pretending that one kind of situation never occurs.

There is, however, a less flattering side to this flexibility. Because a proverb can be found to support almost any course of action, proverbs are well suited to justifying decisions after they have been made. The person who rushed in and succeeded quotes the saying about hesitation; had the venture failed, an onlooker would have been ready with the one about looking first. Used this way, the stock of proverbs becomes a device for making every outcome seem to have been foreseeable.

The two uses are hard to tell apart from the outside, since the same words serve both. The difference lies in timing and in honesty: whether the saying is brought to the situation before the choice, as a way of thinking about it, or fitted to the result afterwards, as a way of not having to. A simple test is to ask whether the speaker could have said in advance which saying they would reach for. If so, the proverb did some work; if the choice was settled only by how things turned out, it did none.
